The elderly King Peter went with them, and Putnik, too ill to walk, was carried in a sedan chair. Tens of thousands of civilians followed, along with Austro-Hungarian prisoners of war.

In deep snow and bitter cold, without adequate food, the columns were decimated by exposure, hunger and typhus, and some were attacked by hostile Albanian tribesmen. Those who reached the coast at Scutari, San Giovanni di Medua and Durazzo found little food waiting, and the Allies argued over how to move them. From January 1916 Italian, French and British ships evacuated the survivors, some 140,000–150,000 soldiers, to the Greek island of Corfu. Many were too weak to recover; so many died on the islet of Vido that bodies were buried at sea.

Re-equipped by the French, the Serbian army was sent to the Salonika front in 1916.
significance: The retreat became Serbia's national epic of suffering and survival. The army's preservation kept Serbia in the war and gave it a claim to a leading role in the Yugoslav state created in 1918.
uncertaintyNote: The numbers who set out, died and were evacuated are all uncertain; estimates of the dead range from tens of thousands to well over 100,000 including civilians.
sources: Andrej Mitrović, Serbia's Great War 1914–1918 (2007)
Hew Strachan, The First World War (2003)
Alan Palmer, The Gardeners of Salonika (1965)

title: Evacuation of Gallipoli
place: Anzac, Suvla and Cape Helles, Gallipoli peninsula, Ottoman Empire (Turkey)
casualties: Almost none during the evacuation itself. For the whole campaign, Allied c. 250,000–300,000 casualties and Ottoman c. 250,000–300,000, with c. 45,000 Allied and c. 55,000–85,000 Ottoman dead
summary: In the one well-executed operation of the campaign, the Allies secretly withdraw from Anzac and Suvla in December and from Cape Helles in January, leaving the Ottoman defenders in possession of the peninsula.
detail:
After the failure of the August offensive and Bulgaria's entry into the war, which opened a direct rail link from Germany to Constantinople and heavy guns for the Ottomans, the Gallipoli bridgeheads had no future. Hamilton's successor, General Sir Charles Monro, recommended evacuation soon after arriving in late October, and Kitchener, visiting in November, reluctantly agreed. A blizzard in late November killed and crippled hundreds of men in the open trenches at Suvla.

The withdrawal from Anzac and Suvla was carried out over successive nights, ending on 19–20 December. Troops left in silence with muffled boots, while self-firing 'drip rifles' and a thinning garrison kept up the appearance of normal activity. Cape Helles, where the Ottomans were now expecting an evacuation, followed on the night of 8–9 January 1916. In both, some 100,000 men were taken off with almost no loss.

The Allies had held the peninsula for eight and a half months.
significance: Gallipoli ended in Allied failure and Ottoman victory, damaging Churchill's career and strengthening Mustafa Kemal's; it deepened national consciousness in Australia, New Zealand and Turkey alike.
uncertaintyNote: Total casualty figures for the campaign vary widely by source, especially Ottoman figures, which range from c. 160,000 to over 250,000 including sick.
sources: Robin Prior, Gallipoli: The End of the Myth (2009)
Edward J. Erickson, Gallipoli: The Ottoman Campaign (2010)
C.E.W. Bean, The Story of Anzac, vol. 2 (Official History of Australia in the War, 1924)
Peter Hart, Gallipoli (2011)

title: Conquest of Montenegro
place: Mount Lovćen and Cetinje, Kingdom of Montenegro
summary: Austro-Hungarian troops storm Mount Lovćen above the Bay of Kotor and take the Montenegrin capital, Cetinje. King Nicholas flees to Italy and his army capitulates.
detail:
Montenegro, Serbia's small ally, had fought alongside it since 1914, and its army covered the Serbian retreat to the coast in the winter of 1915–16, notably at Mojkovac in early January. Its artillery on Mount Lovćen had long overlooked the Austro-Hungarian naval base in the Bay of Kotor.

On 8 January 1916 General Hermann Kövess's Third Army, supported by warships in the bay, began an assault on the Lovćen massif. After three days of fighting in snow and rock the Montenegrins abandoned the mountain, and Austro-Hungarian troops entered Cetinje on 13 January. King Nicholas opened negotiations, then left the country for Italy, while his government and army capitulated later in the month. Austro-Hungarian forces went on to occupy northern and central Albania.

Nicholas's departure, and doubts over his conduct in the surrender talks, discredited the Petrović dynasty. In 1918 Montenegro was absorbed into the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and the king was deposed.
significance: The fall of Montenegro completed the Central Powers' conquest of the western Balkans and secured the Bay of Kotor as a base for Austro-Hungarian and German submarines in the Mediterranean.
uncertaintyNote: The exact date of the Montenegrin capitulation is given variously in late January 1916, as the negotiations were confused.
sources: Holger Herwig, The First World War: Germany and Austria-Hungary 1914–1918 (1997)
Hew Strachan, The First World War (2003)
Elizabeth Roberts, Realm of the Black Mountain: A History of Montenegro (2007)
